'''''Bischofia javanica''''', or '''bishop wood''', is a [[plant]] [[species]] of the [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] [[Phyllanthaceae]]. It and the related ''[[Bischofia polycarpa]]'' are the only two members of [[genus]] ''[[Bischofia]]'' and [[tribe (biology)|tribe]] [[Bischofieae]]. These species are distributed throughout [[South Asia|southern]] and [[southeast Asia]] to [[Australia]] and [[Polynesia]] also in [[North America]] (brought to North America as a decorative plant but now considered to be an invasive species). The tree is commonly used by [[tiger]]s to [[territorial marking|scratch-mark territory]] in the jungles of [[Assam]] where it is locally called ''uriam''. ==Uses==
* The dark red, dense wood is used as a building material for items ranging from furniture to bridges; it is durable but is difficult to air-dry. It is also ideal as firewood.<ref name=":0" />
* The fruits are used in making [[wine]].
* The seeds, which are edible, contain 30–54% oil, which is used as a lubricant.
* The bark has a high tannin content and is used as a source of red [[dye]] to stain rattan baskets<ref>Gardner, Simon, Pindar Sidisunthorn, and Vilaiwan Anusarnsunthorn. A Field Guide to Forest Trees of Northern Thailand. Bangkok: Kobfai Publishing Project, 2000.</ref> and colour [[tapa cloth]].<ref name=":0">{{cite book |last1=Keppel |first1=Gunnar |title=Trees of Fiji: A Guide to 100 Rainforest Trees |last2=Ghazanfar |first2=Shahina A. |author-link2=Shahina A. Ghazanfar |date=2011 |publisher=Secretariat of the Pacific Community & Deutsche Gesellschaft für Technische Zusammenarbeit |edition=third, revised |pages=138–9}}</ref>
* The roots are used [[medicinal]]ly.<ref name='USDA'/>
* The leaves are eaten in Southern Laos dipped into chili sauce.
